claim: Full reliance on AI automation for penetration testing fell from 29% to 9% year-over-year, with 47% of teams moving to a hybrid model.
stance_target: fully autonomous AI agents can replace human review in security testing without quality loss
scope_conditions: Cobalt AI and Pentesting Pulse Report 2026, 455 security leaders/practitioners surveyed, published June 2026
quoted_support: the share of organizations relying entirely on AI automation dropped from 29% year over year, while 47% moved to a hybrid model.

claim: 78% of security teams have experienced false negatives from automated penetration testing tools.
stance_target: automated security sweeps require adversarial/human review layers to catch missed findings
scope_conditions: Cobalt Pulse 2026 survey; true rate likely higher since undetected misses cannot be counted
quoted_support: 78% of security teams have experienced false negatives from automated penetration testing tools.

claim: OWASP's Autonomous Penetration Testing Standard (APTS) defines 8 governance domains across 3 cumulative conformance tiers totaling 173 requirements for autonomous security agents.
stance_target: rigid, tiered governance frameworks (zero-hallucination/quality control pillar) are needed for autonomous agent security actions
quoted_support: APTS defines eight governance domains, with conformance in three cumulative tiers totaling 173 requirements: Scope Enforcement... Safety Controls and Impact Management... Human Oversight and Intervention... Graduated Autonomy Levels... Auditability and Reproducibility... Manipulation Resistance... Third-Party and Supply Chain Trust... Reporting.

claim: No major compliance framework (PCI DSS, FedRAMP, DORA, NCSC CHECK) accepts a fully automated AI penetration test as the complete test; SOC 2 is the one structural exception because its Trust Services Criteria only require reproducible evidence signed by a named human.
stance_target: human-in-the-loop sign-off remains legally/structurally required for autonomous agent output in regulated domains
scope_conditions: PCI DSS 11.4, DORA Article 27, NCSC CHECK, SOC 2 CC4.1, as of August 2026
quoted_support: "No major compliance framework currently accepts a fully automated AI pen test at the time of this writing... Not FedRAMP, PCI DSS, or any of the other standards our clients are regularly assessed against."

claim: XBOW's autonomous agent topped HackerOne's US leaderboard in June 2025, but human staff reviewed submissions before posting per HackerOne's AI-tooling policy -- the widely cited 'fully autonomous' result was actually a hybrid outcome.
stance_target: AI agents have already achieved fully unsupervised superiority over human experts in security testing
quoted_support: The detail that gets dropped is that human staff reviewed the submissions before they went in, to comply with HackerOne's policy on AI tooling. The headline result was already a hybrid, and nobody reported it that way.

claim: A vendor's automated pentest tool produced 2,600 vulnerabilities over 90 days; a practitioner cleared more than 2,000 and received 1,100 fresh findings, illustrating a growing triage/verification burden ('AI slop') rather than labor savings.
stance_target: automation of security findings reduces human verification workload
quoted_support: A vendor's new tool produced 2,600 vulnerabilities to remediate in ninety days, they cleared more than 2,000, and 1,100 fresh ones landed on the list... They call it AI slop, full of hallucinated critical findings.

claim: A recommended penetration-testing requirement should include 10 vendor-neutral clauses: declared autonomy tier per environment, defined triggers, in-finding proof, named human signer, false-positive ceiling, multi-role authenticated testing, coverage assertion, seeded-finding acceptance test, pre-execution review of destructive actions, and evidence-handling rules.
stance_target: rigid evals and blast-radius controls for autonomous security agents need codified procurement/governance clauses, not just capability benchmarks
quoted_support: Run a seeded-finding acceptance test: plant known vulnerabilities in a staging copy and measure what the agent missed. This is the only practical answer to the false-negative problem, and it's the clause most vendors will resist.
